1317.title: Mahamudra
1317.hook: the "great seal": resting in the mind's own nature, taught in the Kagyu school
1317.howItsDone: In the Kagyu school, students usually receive Mahamudra instruction from a teacher after preliminary practices, training first in calm, then in looking directly at the mind, and finally in resting in its nature; other Tibetan schools also teach Mahamudra.

segments.voice: Yesterday, debate in the courtyard. Your line: clap and ask. From a loud practice, today, to a quiet one.

Look at the bottom of an old letter from a king. Pressed into red wax is his seal. It doesn't change the words or add a line, but it marks the whole page: this belongs to the king, this is real. Now take that picture somewhere stranger. What if every thought, every sound, every mood you've ever had carried a seal like that, a mark showing what it truly is, and you'd simply never looked at the bottom of the page? The Kagyu school, which you met earlier this year, names its heart practice after that seal. Today: Mahamudra.
screen: `A KING'S SEAL IN RED WAX.` → `IT MARKS THE WHOLE PAGE.` → `WHAT IF EVERY THOUGHT CARRIED ONE?`

segments.voice: First, the name. Mahamudra is Sanskrit: maha, great, and mudra, a seal or a sign. The great seal. Kagyu teachers explain that everything that appears is stamped with the mind's own nature, open and clear. Nothing escapes the seal, so nothing has to be thrown out to find it. Second, the line it comes down. The Kagyu tell a chain of teachers: the Indian master Tilopa taught Naropa, Naropa taught the Tibetan translator Marpa, Marpa taught Milarepa, and Milarepa taught Gampopa. Tradition says Tilopa gave Naropa a song of Mahamudra on the banks of the Ganges, comparing the mind to space: space rests on nothing, and nothing stains it. Other Tibetan schools teach Mahamudra too, but it sits at the heart of the Kagyu. Third, the instruction, which is short. Six pieces of advice attributed to Tilopa are often summed up like this: don't recall the past, don't imagine the future, don't think about now, don't examine, don't control, and rest. Not to blank the mind, but to stop chasing it. Thoughts still come. They're seen for what they are, marked with the seal, and allowed to go. Fourth, how it's actually practiced. Kagyu teachers usually lead students slowly: first steadying the mind, then looking for where a thought comes from and where it goes, and only then resting in what's found. It's taught by a teacher, step by step, not found in a book in one evening. But the image is simple enough to carry all day: you don't have to remove the thought to find what it's stamped with.
screen: `MAHA, GREAT. MUDRA, SEAL.` · `TILOPA TO NAROPA, ON TO GAMPOPA.` · `SIX PIECES OF ADVICE, ENDING IN REST.` · `STEADY, LOOK, THEN REST.` · then, large: `THE GREAT SEAL.`

segments.voice: Sit upright and easy, eyes open, gaze resting softly a little ahead. When a thought appears, don't follow it into the past or the future, and don't push it away: notice it, the way you'd notice a seal at the bottom of a page, and let it go. Then rest in the noticing itself, and if you drift, come back without a fuss.
Mahamudra. The great seal: in Kagyu teaching, resting in the mind's own nature, which marks every thought and appearance. Today's word.
Your line: the great seal. Look at the bottom of the page. See you tomorrow.

1318.title: Dzogchen
1318.hook: the "great perfection" of the Nyingma school: awareness already complete
1318.howItsDone: In the Nyingma school, Dzogchen is taught as the summit of the path: after preliminary practices, a teacher introduces the student to rigpa, the mind's basic awareness, and the student trains in resting in it and letting thoughts free themselves.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mahamudra. Your line: the great seal. Today, its neighbor in the Nyingma school.

A mirror hangs in a hallway. All day, things pass in front of it: a child with a muddy face, a bouquet of flowers, someone crying, someone laughing, a dog. The mirror shows every one of them completely, and when each walks away, it's exactly as it was. The mud didn't dirty it. The flowers didn't make it more beautiful. Nobody had to polish it into being a mirror. It already was one. The Nyingma school of Tibet points at the mind with a picture like this. Today: Dzogchen.
screen: `A MIRROR IN A HALLWAY.` → `IT SHOWS EVERYTHING.` → `NOTHING STAINS IT.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Dzogchen is Tibetan, usually translated the great perfection, or the great completeness. In Nyingma teaching, which you met earlier this year, it's the summit of the whole path, the last of their nine vehicles. Second, the claim, which is bold. Nyingma teachers say the mind's basic awareness, which they call rigpa, is already complete. Practice doesn't manufacture it. Like the mirror, it shows everything, is stained by nothing, and needs nothing added. What we usually call the mind, the running commentary, the worries, the plans, is like the things passing in front of the glass. Third, the three statements. Tradition credits a teacher named Garab Dorje with summing up Dzogchen in three short lines, which the Nyingma master Patrul Rinpoche later explained in a commentary. In plain words: be introduced directly to your own nature. Decide on this one thing, without doubt. Gain confidence that thoughts free themselves as they arise. That last one is the surprise. A thought doesn't have to be fought or fixed. Seen for what it is, it dissolves on its own, like writing on water. Fourth, what that does not mean. Not doing nothing, or drifting, or giving up on kindness. Nyingma teachers say ethics, compassion and the preliminary practices still matter, and that resting in rigpa is very different from spacing out. The ease is the fruit of long preparation. But the starting point is turned around: what's being looked for is already here. Stop covering it up.
screen: `THE GREAT PERFECTION, THE SUMMIT.` · `RIGPA: AWARENESS, LIKE A MIRROR.` · `GARAB DORJE'S THREE STATEMENTS.` · `NOT DRIFTING: PREPARED EASE.` · then, large: `ALREADY COMPLETE.`

segments.voice: Sit with your eyes open and your gaze wide and soft, taking in the whole room without landing anywhere. Whatever shows up, a sound, an itch, a thought about dinner, let it show up the way things show up in a mirror, and don't improve your posture, your breath or your mind. If you catch yourself fixing, notice that too, and rest as the mirror.
Dzogchen. The great perfection of the Nyingma school: the teaching that awareness, rigpa, is already complete, like a mirror nothing can stain. Today's word.
Your line: already complete. Like the mirror, never dirtied by what passes in front of it. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1319.title: Only with a teacher
1319.hook: both Mahamudra and Dzogchen are traditionally learned face to face
1319.howItsDone: In Tibetan Buddhism, Mahamudra and Dzogchen are traditionally received from a qualified teacher, often after preliminary practices, in a pointing-out instruction given in person; teacher and student are advised to examine each other before the relationship begins.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dzogchen. Your line: already complete. Today, how both great teachings are passed on.

Two people stop on a woodland path. One whispers: there's an owl. The other looks. Bark, branches, leaves, more bark. Nothing. The first steps behind, lines up a finger beside the other's cheek, and points. Third branch up. Where it forks. That gray lump. And all at once the lump has eyes and a face, and it can't be unseen. A field guide could have described that owl for a year. It took a person, a finger and a moment, side by side. Tibetan teachers say the deepest teachings pass the same way. Today: only with a teacher.
screen: `THERE'S AN OWL.` → `FOLLOW MY FINGER.` → `NOW IT CAN'T BE UNSEEN.`

segments.voice: First, the pointing out. Both Mahamudra and Dzogchen speak of a moment when a teacher points out the nature of the student's own mind. Yesterday's first statement of Garab Dorje was: be introduced directly to your own nature. An introduction needs someone to make it. The mind's nature, Tibetan teachers explain, is so close and so simple that we look straight past it, the way an eye can't see itself. Second, a story the Kagyu tell, which you first met in year three. Naropa was a great scholar, tradition says, honored for his learning. Then he met the wild teacher Tilopa, who for years put him through hardship after hardship and taught him almost nothing in words. In the story, the moment finally came when Tilopa struck him with a sandal, and Naropa saw. What a lifetime of reading had circled around, one face-to-face moment opened. Third, care on both sides. The guru yoga lesson met the advice to examine a teacher. Here it runs both ways: Tibetan texts on teacher and student advise each to examine the other before the relationship begins. A pointing out only means something from a teacher whose own life shows the teaching. Fourth, what's left for everyone else. Books, recordings and lessons like this one can describe these teachings and prepare the ground. Teachers in both lineages say the rest happens in person. Saying so plainly is part of honoring the teaching.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you only learned because someone showed you, side by side: tying a shoe, riding a bike, a prayer, a recipe, how to be kind to someone who's grieving. See their hands, their face, the moment it clicked, and let some thanks go toward them, wherever they are now.
Only with a teacher. In Tibetan tradition, Mahamudra and Dzogchen are learned face to face, when a trusted teacher points out the nature of the student's mind. Today's word.
Your line: face to face. Some things need a finger beside your cheek, not another page. Until tomorrow.

1320.title: The in-between
1320.hook: the Tibetan teachings on the bardos: dying, the clear light, becoming
1320.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists study the bardo teachings during life, practice with dreams and meditation as preparation, and read texts such as the Bardo Thödol aloud beside the dying and the dead to guide them through the in-between.

segments.voice: Yesterday, only with a teacher, the owl and the pointing finger. Your line: face to face.

High under a circus tent, a trapeze artist swings out on one bar. At the top of the arc, she lets go. For a moment she holds nothing at all: the old bar swinging away behind her, the new one still on its way. Her whole act lives in that half second, because everything depends on what she does with empty hands. Tibetan teachers describe death, and much of life, as a moment like that. You first met their word for it in year one. Today, a closer look: bardo.
screen: `ONE BAR LET GO.` → `EMPTY HANDS IN THE AIR.` → `THE NEXT BAR NOT YET CAUGHT.`

segments.voice: First, the map. Bardo means in-between. Tibetan teachers describe several bardos, some in this life, like dreaming and meditation, and others that come with death. Today, the passage through death as the teachings tell it: dying, the clear light, and becoming. Second, the bardo of dying. Teachers describe the body's powers withdrawing one by one, strength going, warmth fading, the senses dimming, like lamps going out room by room in a house at night. They describe it calmly and in detail, so that someone who has heard it beforehand might recognize what's happening and not be afraid. At the very end, they say, a clear light dawns; that's tomorrow's lesson. Third, the bardo of becoming. If the clear light isn't recognized, the teachings say, visions follow, which come soon. After them comes becoming: the mind, now without a body, pushed by old habits the way a feather is pushed by wind, is drawn toward a new birth. The Bardo Thödol, read aloud beside the dead, speaks to the person at each step, reminding them: these appearances are your own mind. Fourth, why it's taught to the living. Tibetan teachers say every in-between, falling asleep, waking up, the space between one thought and the next, is a small rehearsal. What a person practices in the small gaps, steadiness, recognition, letting go, is what they'll have in the big one. So the in-between isn't only a danger. It's an opening: with nothing held, for a moment, there's room to see clearly, and to catch the next bar well.

Notice how it feels in the body, then rest in the smallest in-between of all, the pause at the bottom of each out-breath, hands open. 1321.title: The clear light
1321.hook: at death, the teachings say, a clear light dawns
1321.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists prepare for death by practicing recognition of the mind's nature in meditation, the 'child' clear light, so that the 'mother' clear light at death may be recognized; the Bardo Thödol is read aloud to remind the one who has died.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bardo. Your line: in between. Today, the light at the end of dying.

A summer night, and the whole city loses power at once. Streetlights, windows, billboards, gone. People stand on their porches, a little uneasy. Then someone looks up and says, oh. Above the rooftops the sky is full of stars, more than anyone on the block has seen there in years. They hadn't arrived. They'd been there the whole time, drowned out by all the other lights. Tibetan teachers say something like that happens at the end of a life: when every other light goes out, something that was always shining shows itself. Today: the clear light.
screen: `THE CITY GOES DARK.` → `THE STARS WERE ALWAYS THERE.` → `WHEN THE OTHER LIGHTS GO OUT.`

segments.voice: First, what the teachings say. At the end of the bardo of dying, when the senses have withdrawn and the breath has stopped, a clear light dawns. Tibetans call it ösel, and teachers describe it like a clear sky, empty of clouds. It isn't a light from outside, they say. It's the mind's own nature, bare. The Bardo Thödol speaks to the person at that moment, by name: this is your own mind. Recognize it. Second, the mother and the child. Glimpses of the mind's nature met in meditation during life are called the child clear light. The clear light at death is called the mother. If the child has been met often enough, they say, the two recognize each other and meet like a child running into its mother's lap. That's why a lifetime of practice matters for this moment. Third, an older echo, the luminous mind you met in year two. In a short Pali discourse, the Buddha says the mind is luminous, stained by defilements that arrive like visitors. Some readers hear the same intuition there: underneath the passing stains, something clear. The two speak in their own ways, and neither needs the other to make its point. Fourth, why this is taught to the living. Teachers say small glimpses come every day: in the gap after a thought, at the edge of sleep, in the moment after a sneeze or a surprise, before the mind starts talking again. The practice, in this teaching, is learning to notice the stars before the lights go out.

1322.title: Peaceful and wrathful
1322.hook: the visions of the bardo, recognized as the mind's own display
1322.howItsDone: In Tibetan Buddhism, peaceful and wrathful figures appear in temple paintings and in the bardo texts, and teachers explain them as forms of awakened mind that the dead, and the living, are asked to recognize rather than fear.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the clear light: the teaching that at death a bright, open awareness dawns, and the task is to know it. Your line: the clear light.

Inside a Tibetan temple, the wall paintings go all the way around. On one side, calm figures sit on lotuses, gentle faces, soft colors, hands resting in their laps. A few steps along, the mood changes: dark blue and red bodies, flaming hair, bared teeth, crowns of skulls, a stance like they're about to stamp the ground. It feels like a walk from a garden into a storm. Both walls belong to the same teaching. In the Tibetan texts of the in-between, these are the figures that appear after death, and the instruction that comes with them is short and startling.
screen: `CALM FACES ON LOTUSES.` → `FLAMES, FANGS, A STAMPING FOOT.` → `ONE TEACHING, TWO WALLS.`

segments.voice: The Bardo Thodol, known in English as the Tibetan Book of the Dead, describes what the one who has died meets in the in-between. If the clear light passes unrecognized, visions follow. First come peaceful figures, buddhas of light, radiant and kind. Then, as the text tells it, the same figures return in wrathful form, fierce and terrifying. Here's the surprise. The text doesn't tell the dead person to fight these beings, or run, or plead with them. It says, again and again: recognize them. They are not visitors from outside. They are the display of your own mind, the calm ones and the fierce ones alike. Why fierce at all? In Tibetan teaching, a wrathful figure is not a demon. It is compassion with its sleeves rolled up: the energy that cuts through confusion, the way a parent shouts when a child steps toward a road. The fierceness is aimed at what blocks waking up, never at the one who's waking. Some teachers in this tradition point out that people live through small versions of this all the time. A mood rises, gentle or furious, and it seems to come from out there: the email, the driver, the weather. The bardo teaching asks a simpler question first. Whose mind is showing this? Recognition, the text says, is enough. Some readers take the visions quite literally; others hear them mainly as a map of the mind. The text holds both.

1323.title: Read to the dying
1323.hook: the text is read aloud to the dying and the dead
1323.howItsDone: In Tibetan communities, a lama, monk or trained friend may read the Bardo Thodol aloud beside someone who is dying and continue reading after death, speaking directly to the one who has died through the days of the in-between.

segments.voice: Yesterday, peaceful and wrathful: calm figures and fierce ones, and one instruction for both. Your line: your own mind.

A small room, the lamps low. Someone has just died, or is very close to it. Beside the bed sits a monk, or a family friend who knows how, with a long, narrow book on their knees: loose pages printed in Tibetan, held between two boards. And they are reading out loud. Not to the family, though the family hears it. Not to themselves. They are reading to the person who is dying, and they will keep reading after the breathing stops. That is what this book was made for.
screen: `A LOW-LIT ROOM.` → `A BOOK ON SOMEONE'S KNEES.` → `READ TO THE ONE WHO IS DYING.`

segments.voice: The book is the Bardo Thodol, which means liberation through hearing in the in-between. Hearing: the whole name rests on it. It isn't mainly a book for scholars to study at a desk. It is a book to be spoken into someone's ear. The reader addresses the one who has died by name, the way a guide talks to a traveler on a dark road: this is the clear light, recognize it. These visions are your own mind; don't be afraid. Tradition holds that awareness goes on hearing after the body has gone quiet, so the reading goes on too, through the days of the in-between. Where did it come from? Tibetan tradition says Padmasambhava taught it and hid it as a treasure, and that a treasure-revealer, Karma Lingpa, brought it to light long afterward. And it isn't only for the dead. Some teachers say it's meant to be heard long before the end, read in life, so the words are already familiar when they're needed most. It shapes the living in the room too: someone sitting by a deathbed, with nothing to fix, is given something to do with their voice. Look back across this week: the great seal and the great perfection, the teacher face to face, the in-between, the clear light, the two walls of visions. All of it, in the end, carried by a human voice reading aloud. And if a loss is heavy on you right now and you feel in danger, call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency help.
screen: `LIBERATION THROUGH HEARING.` · `SPOKEN TO THE ONE WHO DIED.` · `A HIDDEN TREASURE, TRADITION SAYS.` · `READ IN LIFE, HEARD AT THE END.` · then, large: `READ ALOUD.`
